---
title: "Molecules, radiation, and climate exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Compare wavelengths

For the two teaching bands in the notes, calculate absorbed fractions. Can you conclude that the gas absorbs more total energy in the 10 µm band without knowing the incident spectrum?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Absorbed power depends on both absorption fraction and incident power.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The fractions are **0.05** and **0.80** in the absorbing-only example. Total absorbed power also requires the incident energy in each band and their widths. Fractions alone cannot establish an integrated energy budget.
:::

## 2. An infrared-active mode

Why is the statement “CO₂ is symmetric, so it cannot absorb infrared” incorrect? Contrast an active CO₂ mode with N₂ vibration.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Consider the changing dipole during vibration, not only the resting structure.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The CO₂ asymmetric stretch and bending motions change dipole moment and can absorb infrared. Ordinary N₂ vibration does not create that changing molecular dipole. Other weak absorption mechanisms do not reverse this basic comparison.
:::

## 3. A constructed gas sink

A fictitious gas has a fixed first-order loss coefficient k = 0.0200 day⁻¹. Calculate its lifetime, half-life, and remaining fraction after 50.0 days.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use 1/k, ln(2)/k, and exp(−kt).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Lifetime **50.0 days**; half-life **34.7 days**; remaining fraction **e⁻¹ = 0.368**. These describe the stated one-sink model, not CO₂ or a complete atmospheric transport system.
:::

## 4. Compare two emissions

Two emitted gases have equal mass and different absorption bands and lifetimes. What information would you need to compare their climate effects?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Mass alone omits molecular number, radiation, chemistry, and timescale.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
You need molecular masses, spectroscopic absorption, atmospheric abundance and overlap, chemical removal, distribution, and a stated comparison time horizon. Aerosol or chemical indirect effects can also matter. Equal emitted mass does not imply equal forcing.
:::

## Explore: how long a pulse stays in the air {#explore}

Predict which has more left after 100 years: a CO₂ pulse or a pulse of a gas
with one sink and a 12-year lifetime. Then move the time and the lifetime and
compare the two curves.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="co2pulse" role="group" aria-label="Pulse decay: one sink compared with carbon dioxide">
<p>Reference case: after 100 years about 0.41 of a CO₂ pulse is still in the air, compared with less than 0.001 for a gas with one sink and a 12-year lifetime.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/co2pulse.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Lifetime 50, read at 50**. Check the rate constant, half-life
and fraction left by hand. Compare with exercise 3, which used days instead of
years. Why are the numbers the same?

**E2.** Choose **After 20 years**, then **Lecture comparison** and **After 500
years**. At which times does the CO₂ pulse have more left than the 12-year gas?
Use the table to say which part of the CO₂ pulse is responsible.

**E3.** Raise the one-sink lifetime until its curve is close to the CO₂ curve
at 20 years. Then look at 500 years. Explain why no single lifetime can match
the CO₂ curve at all times.

### Model conditions and hand check

For one first-order sink, `fraction left = e^(−t/τ)`, `k = 1/τ` and
`half-life = 0.693 τ`. With τ = 50 years and t = 50 years: k = **0.0200 per
year**, half-life **34.7 years**, fraction left `e⁻¹ =` **0.368**. The fraction
depends only on t/τ, so exercise 3's 50 days and 50 days give the same numbers.

The CO₂ curve is the impulse-response fit of Joos et al. (2013), used in the IPCC
Fifth Assessment Report:
`0.217 + 0.224 e^(−t/394.4) + 0.282 e^(−t/36.54) + 0.276 e^(−t/4.304)`, with t in
years. It gives about **0.60** left after 20 years, **0.41** after 100 years and
**0.28** after 500 years. The 12-year gas has `e^(−100/12) = 0.0002` left after
100 years.

The fit describes one small pulse added to present-day air, as simulated by
carbon-cycle models. Its four parts are fitted terms, not separate measured
reservoirs, and the constant part is only constant over the centuries the fit
covers; weathering and carbonate reactions remove it over many thousands of
years. The one-sink gas is constructed for comparison: no transport, no change
in sink strength and no chemical side effects.
